scenes.narration: A staircase, and you're counting the ways up. A hundred million recalculations, or forty additions.
Pattern eight of ten in the NBX Studio Dojo: Dynamic Programming. The one everybody's frightened of, which is really just refusing to solve the same thing twice.

scenes.headline: The words that [give it away]
scenes.caption: signals in the question
scenes.narration: Three phrasings cover most of it. ^Number of ways, which is counting rather than listing. ^Minimum or maximum cost, where you're optimising. ^Longest or shortest something. ^And the real test: can the answer for n be built from answers to smaller versions of n? ^If the question wants the actual list rather than a count, that's backtracking from the previous pattern. ^And if a locally best choice is always globally right, greedy is cheaper. Counting, optimising, and built from smaller answers. Those three together mean dynamic programming.
scenes.premise: Words lifted straight out of the question, and the pattern each one points at. Red means the signal rules this pattern OUT.

scenes.headline: Five stairs, [how many ways?]
scenes.caption: the question
scenes.narration: You're climbing a staircase of five steps, and each move is either one step or two. How many different ways are there to reach the top? Your first instinct is to try every possibility, and for five stairs that's fine: ^stair one, ^stair two, ^stair three, ^stair four, ^stair five, and the answer comes out at eight. But try that on forty stairs and your laptop will still be thinking about it tomorrow, because the work doubles with every stair.
scenes.premise: A staircase of five steps. Each box is one stair, and the number written in it is how many different ways there are to reach that stair.

scenes.headline: Two things, [every time]
scenes.caption: base cases and a recurrence
scenes.narration: Every dynamic programming problem needs two things, and finding them is genuinely the whole job. First the base cases: the smallest problems you know without thinking. |One stair has ^one way. Two stairs has ^two ways, two singles or one double. %Those are given, not derived. Second the recurrence: how a bigger answer is built from smaller ones. %To land on stair n you came from n minus one or from n minus two. So the ways to reach n are those two added, and that sentence is what you hunt for every time.

lines.detail: The two smallest staircases you know by heart.

scenes.premise: A staircase of five steps. Each box is one stair, and the number written in it is how many different ways there are to reach that stair.

scenes.headline: Two [sticky notes]
scenes.caption: all the memory you need
scenes.narration: |Prev2 equals one and prev1 equals two, and those are two sticky notes: %prev2 remembers ^the stair two below, %and prev1 remembers ^the stair one below. Why two notes and not a whole table? Because the recurrence never looks back further than two places, so anything older can be thrown away. Most people write this with a full array first, which is fine, but noticing you need only two variables is what drops the space to constant.

lines.detail: Two sticky notes: one stair back, and two stairs back.

scenes.premise: A staircase of five steps. Each box is one stair, and the number written in it is how many different ways there are to reach that stair.

scenes.headline: Building stair [three]
scenes.caption: the first derived answer
scenes.narration: |The loop starts at stair three, because one and two are already known. |Current equals prev1 plus prev2, so two plus one is ^three ways to reach stair three. |Then the notes slide forward: prev2 takes prev1's old value, |and prev1 takes the answer we just computed. %Prev2 is two now, %and prev1 is three. That slide is where people slip, because the order matters: overwrite prev1 first and you've destroyed the number prev2 was about to take.

lines.detail: Start at three: one and two are already known.
The new answer is the two below it, added.
...in this order, or you lose a value.

scenes.premise: A staircase of five steps. Each box is one stair, and the number written in it is how many different ways there are to reach that stair.

scenes.narration: ^Straight from the Dojo. Stair three takes three ways and stair two takes two ways. So how many ways to reach stair four? ^Four ways. ^Five ways. ^Six ways. ^Or three ways. Have a think, and pause the video if you'd like a moment. ^Ready? Five, because three plus two is five, and every route to stair four arrived from one of those two stairs below it.

quiz.question: Stair 3 = 3 ways, stair 2 = 2 ways. Stair 4?
quiz.why: Every route to stair 4 came from stair 3 or stair 2.

scenes.headline: Four, then [five]
scenes.caption: the table fills once
scenes.narration: |Stair four is three plus two, which is ^five ways, and the notes slide again. |Stair five is five plus three, which is ^eight ways. %That's our answer. Five stairs, and we did five additions. Every stair was computed exactly once and then only read, which is the whole point of the pattern.
scenes.premise: A staircase of five steps. Each box is one stair, and the number written in it is how many different ways there are to reach that stair.

scenes.headline: It was [Fibonacci] all along
scenes.caption: one, two, three, five, eight
scenes.narration: Look at the numbers we produced: ^one, ^two, ^three, ^five, ^eight. That's the Fibonacci sequence, and climbing stairs is Fibonacci wearing a hat. A surprising number of dynamic programming problems turn out to be a famous sequence in disguise, and spotting that's often faster than deriving anything. If you write out the first few answers by hand and the pattern looks familiar, trust it and check it.
scenes.premise: A staircase of five steps. Each box is one stair, and the number written in it is how many different ways there are to reach that stair.

scenes.headline: Why the [recursion] hurts
scenes.caption: the same work, over and over
scenes.narration: Here's what dynamic programming saves you from. Written as plain recursion, stair five asks for four and three, stair four asks for three and two, so stair three gets computed twice before we've properly started. ^Stair ten costs about a hundred and eighty calls. ^Stair forty costs over three hundred million, nearly all recomputing answers the program already had. ^The loop does forty additions. ^Same recurrence either way, because the only difference is whether you write down what you worked out.
scenes.premise: The same job priced two ways as the input grows: the obvious method against the pattern. Longer bar means more work.

scenes.headline: How to actually [find it]
scenes.caption: the recipe, in order
scenes.narration: When a dynamic programming question lands and your mind goes blank, do these in order. ^Brute force the answers for n equals one, two, three and four by hand. ^Then ask how each relates to the ones before it, because that relationship is your recurrence. ^Pin down the base cases. ^Write the loop upward from them. ^And only then ask whether the array can shrink to a couple of variables. Order matters, because optimising space before the recurrence is correct is how people burn twenty minutes and end up with neither.

scenes.narration: Three things to take with you. The signal is %counting or optimising, built from smaller answers. You always need %a recurrence and base cases, and neither one alone is enough. And the saving comes from %solving each subproblem once, then only reading it.
Next in the Dojo is greedy, which is what you get when the locally best choice happens to be the globally right one, and no table is needed at all. Go and do Climbing Stairs first.
